questions.prompt: What does Chapter 15 mean by productivity?
choices: Carrying the chosen priority forward through concentrated execution
Keeping as many worthwhile tasks moving as possible
Clearing visible work so the day feels full

explanation.gentle: The chapter defines productivity as carrying the chosen first claim forward.
explanation.direct: Productivity means execution shaped by priority.
explanation.competitive: The winner has to keep the field.

questions.prompt: Why can a clear priority still fail in practice?
choices: Because the day can still scatter force across noise and side tasks
Because priority only matters after commitment is complete
Because productivity is unrelated to execution

explanation.gentle: Priority can stay abstract if the day keeps feeding noise.
explanation.direct: A named priority still fails if action does not gather around it.
explanation.competitive: The winner can still starve if the field scatters.

questions.prompt: Which situation best matches Chapter 15's idea of productivity?
choices: Answering many messages before starting the real work
Keeping multiple small tasks alive so momentum feels high
Giving the next serious work block to the priority that already has first claim

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants the right thing to keep the real block of effort.
explanation.direct: Productivity means concentrated execution on the chosen priority.
explanation.competitive: The winner has to get the block, not applause.

questions.prompt: In the school examples, what makes a study block productive?
choices: Switching often so more checklist items move
Spending equal time on every open subject
Letting the most important exam or paper keep the timer block long enough to deepen

explanation.gentle: A productive study block stays with the work that matters most.
explanation.direct: The key is concentrated execution on the highest-priority subject.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter reject as output theater?
choices: Deep work on the main initiative
Visible motion that leaves the first claim mostly untouched
Protecting a block from side-task drift

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that visible activity can still avoid the main work.
explanation.direct: Output theater is scattered motion that looks productive.
explanation.competitive: Busy noise is not a win.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 15 build on Chapter 14?
choices: It replaces priority with a looser idea of effort
It asks whether the chosen first claim now governs execution
It delays action until all commitments are named

explanation.gentle: Chapter 14 names first claim, and Chapter 15 asks whether action follows it.
explanation.direct: The move is from priority to concentrated execution.
explanation.competitive: The winner now has to take the field.

questions.prompt: What is the personal-life version of productivity in this chapter?
choices: Giving the evening hour to the personal move that matters most
Finishing as many chores as possible before resting
Keeping every good intention active at once

explanation.gentle: Personal productivity means the right move receives the hour.
explanation.direct: The evening should reflect the first claim, not just stay busy.
explanation.competitive: The winner has to own the hour.

questions.prompt: What harder standard does the chapter use to judge a day?
choices: Whether the calendar looked full
Whether the chosen priority kept receiving the best force
Whether many small tasks were completed

explanation.gentle: The chapter judges the day by whether the right priority kept the force.
explanation.direct: A productive day is one where first claim stays in charge of action.
explanation.competitive: The field only counts if the winner kept control.

questions.prompt: Why can a day with fewer completions still be more productive?
choices: Because unfinished work is always a better signal
Because deep movement on the right priority can matter more than broad motion
Because visible output should never matter at all

explanation.gentle: Fewer completions can still be better if the right thing advanced.
explanation.direct: Concentrated progress on first claim outweighs scattered motion.
explanation.competitive: A smaller board can still win if the winner moved.

questions.prompt: What question does Chapter 15 leave for Chapter 16?
choices: How can more tasks be kept active at the same time?
How can productivity be measured by volume alone?
What commitments are required to protect concentrated execution?

explanation.gentle: The chapter points toward the commitments needed to protect concentration.
explanation.direct: It leaves the reader asking how first-claim execution can be defended under pressure.
explanation.competitive: The winner needs protection if it is going to stay on the field.
